did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a prophetic formula: the word of the Lord comes to Jeremiah and directs his actions.
Jeremiah sees the potter working at the potter’s wheel and shaping a vessel from clay.
When the vessel is spoiled in the potter’s hands, he does not discard the clay; instead, he makes it into another vessel, as he sees fit.
The Lord uses the image of the potter and the clay as a metaphor for His relationship with Israel: just as the clay is in the potter’s hands, so Israel is in the Lord’s hands.
The chapter teaches that a judgment of disaster is not always presented as irreversible: if a nation turns from its evil, the Lord may relent from the disaster He had announced against it.
A promise of blessing is also tied to behavior: if the people do evil and do not obey the Lord, the blessing promised to them may be withdrawn.
Jeremiah is commanded to warn Judah and Jerusalem and call everyone to turn from their evil ways and change their conduct and actions.
The people’s response to this appeal is an outright refusal: they say they will follow their own plans and act according to the stubbornness of their evil hearts.
Jeremiah’s opponents claim that his words are unnecessary because, in their view, instruction comes from the priest, counsel from the wise, and the word from the prophet.
Jeremiah reminds the Lord that he had previously stood before Him and pleaded for Him to turn away His anger from the people, even though they are now repaying him with evil for good.
